title: Research Use of Medicare Prescription Drug Event (PDE) Data
text:
What Is PDE Data?
PDE = Prescription Drug Event — the record of prescription-drug fills under Medicare Part D.

Whenever a Part D beneficiary fills a prescription, the plan submits a PDE record summarizing the fill event
PDE data are standardized — not raw transactional claims but CMS-defined summary extracts

title: Research Use of Medicare Prescription Drug Event (PDE) Data
section: Why PDE Matters / Who Reports It
text:
Why PDE Matters / Who Reports It

All Part D plan sponsors (stand-alone PDPs and Medicare Advantage plans with drug benefits) must report PDE data to CMS for every covered fill
Provides a comprehensive view of outpatient prescription drug utilization among Medicare beneficiaries under Part D

title: Research Use of Medicare Prescription Drug Event (PDE) Data
section: What PDE Captures — And What It Doesn’t
text:
What PDE Captures — And What It Doesn’t


✅ What it captures:

Detailed outpatient prescription drug fills under Part D
Timing, drug identity, strength, quantity, payment data
Enables utilization, adherence, cost, and drug-exposure analyses


⚠️ Limitations:

Drugs administered during hospitalizations may not appear
Dispensed ≠ ingested (no guarantee drug was taken)
Limited clinical context — must link with other Medicare files
Doesn’t capture drugs not covered by Part D (OTC, hospital-administered)

title: Research Use of Medicare Prescription Drug Event (PDE) Data
text:
How Researchers Use PDE Data

Define medication exposure periods — when a drug was filled, days supply
Study drug utilization patterns — adherence (MPR, gaps), polypharmacy
Link with Medicare claims — inpatient, outpatient, diagnoses for health outcomes, safety, pharmacoepidemiology
Cost and utilization analyses — what drugs, how often, cost burden, subsidies

title: A Powerful Post-Estimation Tool in Stata: Margins
section: When to Use the margins Command?
text:
When to Use the margins Command?
For more complex models in Stata, it is often easier to interpret margins — specifically, margins of responses or margins of changes in responses.

Margins are statistics calculated from predictions of a previously fit model at fixed values of some covariates and averaging over the remaining covariates.

Margins answers: “What does my model have to say about such-and-such a group or such-and-such a person?”

title: A Powerful Post-Estimation Tool in Stata: Margins
text:
Types of Margins of Responses








Abbreviation
Name
Description




APM
Average Predictive Margins
Average of responses among actual people in the data


PMM
Predictive Margins at the Means
Expected response for a person with average characteristics


PMR
Predictive Margins at Representative Values
Expected response across a range of covariate values

title: A Powerful Post-Estimation Tool in Stata: Margins
section: Types of Margins of Changes in Responses
text:
Types of Margins of Changes in Responses








Abbreviation
Name
Description




AME
Average Marginal Effects
Average of changes in responses among actual people


MEM
Marginal Effects at the Means
Expected change for a person with average characteristics


MER
Marginal Effects at Representative Values
Expected change across a range of covariate values

title: A Powerful Post-Estimation Tool in Stata: Margins
section: Where to Use the margins Command?
text:
Where to Use the margins Command?

The margins command can only be used after running a regression — it acts on the most recent regression results
The marginsplot command graphs any margins or comparisons of margins — it acts on the most recent margins results

regress y x1 x2 x3
margins
marginsplot

title: A Powerful Post-Estimation Tool in Stata: Margins
text:
Example Data: NHANES II
Margins of Responses Example
Predicting continuous systolic blood pressure (bpsystol) as a function of:

Age (age)
Diabetes status (diabetes)
Geographic region (region)

Using OLS regression

Dataset: NHANES II (Second National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, mid-to-late 1970s) wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/nhanes2

title: A Powerful Post-Estimation Tool in Stata: Margins
text:
Average Predictive Margins (APM)
The mean predicted value of systolic blood pressure is 130.89, based on each observation in the data.
regress bpsystol age i.diabetes i.region
margins

APM gives the average of the predicted values across all actual observations.

Marginal Effects at the Means (MEM)
margins, dydx(*) atmeans

Calculate marginal effects with all other covariates fixed at their sample means

title: A Powerful Post-Estimation Tool in Stata: Margins
text:
Margins with Interactions
Research question: Does marital status (marital) affect the relationship between sex and general happiness (happy), controlling for income (rincome) and education (educ)?
mlogit happy i.sex##i.marital rincome educ
margins marital, at(sex=(0 1))
marginsplot

Dataset: General Social Survey (GSS) — gss.norc.org


⚠️ Interpretation of interactions in multinomial logit models can be tricky — use margins to make results interpretable.

title: A Powerful Post-Estimation Tool in Stata: Margins
text:
Margins with Interactions: Results
Fixing income and education at specific levels:

Different marital statuses have different predicted probabilities of happiness compared to the base category
marginsplot visualizes these predicted probabilities across groups

title: A Powerful Post-Estimation Tool in Stata: Margins
text:
Example: Margins with Dummy Variables
Research question: Does depression affect the relationship between serious illness and 90-day Medicare expenditure post-surgery?
glm tot_paid_by_mc_p90 i.ind_depression##i.ind_si_any, family(gamma) link(log)
margins ind_depression#ind_si_any

Project work using Medpar data linked to HRS data


⚠️ Default regression output coefficients do not directly translate to dollar amounts — use margins to get interpretable results

text:

margins ind_depression#ind_si_any
marginsplot, recast(bar) by(ind_si_any)

title: ADRD Drug Repurposing Study
text:
This ongoing study leverages large-scale CMS Medicare claims data to identify candidate drugs for repurposing in Alzheimer’s Disease and Related Dementias (ADRD). As lead analyst, I am responsible for the full analytical pipeline — from data extraction and harmonization through causal inference modeling and results interpretation.
Drug repurposing using real-world claims data offers a powerful, cost-effective approach to identifying existing medications that may slow cognitive decline or reduce ADRD-related outcomes in older adults.

title: About
text:
I’m a senior research scientist in the Brookdale Department of Geriatrics and Palliative Care at Mount Sinai Hospital, where I’ve spent 5+ years working with large-scale CMS Medicare and Medicaid claims data to study aging, ADRD, and emergency and hospital visit outcomes.
My core expertise is in CMS Medicare and Medicaid data — from raw claims ingestion and harmonization through to analysis and results interpretation. I’ve built pipelines and models using Stata and R, applying methods including regression, longitudinal analysis, survival modeling, and causal inference frameworks.
I currently serve as lead biostatistician on a WTC first responders frailty study, lead analyst on an ADRD drug repurposing project using CMS claims, and biostatistician on a randomized controlled trial of a palliative care at home intervention.
I’m currently in a deliberate transition toward health data science and applied machine learning — combining my domain expertise and analytical rigor with modern ML methods. I’m actively building Python skills, exploring gradient boosting and survival ML models, and developing literacy in explainability tools for clinical deployment contexts.

title: WTC First Responders Frailty Study
text:
Status: Ongoing | Role: Lead Biostatistician | Software: Stata


This repository contains the statistical analysis code for a longitudinal study examining frailty trajectories among World Trade Center (WTC) first responders. The study investigates frailty prevalence, predictors, risk factors, and health outcomes in this well-characterized cohort with long-term follow-up data.




What is the prevalence of frailty in WTC first responders, and how has it changed over time?
What are the key predictors and risk factors for frailty in this population?
How does frailty relate to downstream health outcomes including hospitalizations, functional decline, and mortality?




Longitudinal / repeated measures — participants assessed at multiple time points enabling analysis of frailty onset, progression, and reversal over time.




Descriptive statistics (frailty prevalence and sample characteristics)
Longitudinal regression (frailty trajectories over time)
Mixed effects models (within-person change)
Survival analysis (time to frailty onset and outcomes)
Causal inference (effect of WTC exposures on frailty risk)




wtc-frailty/
├── 01_data_cleaning/       # Data harmonization and cleaning scripts
├── 02_descriptive/         # Descriptive statistics and tables
├── 03_longitudinal/        # Mixed effects and trajectory models
├── 04_survival/            # Time-to-event analyses
├── 05_causal/              # Causal inference models
├── 06_sensitivity/         # Sensitivity and robustness analyses
└── notes/                  # Analytical decision notes and SAP



All scripts are written in Stata. Run in order (01 → 06). Each script includes inline comments explaining analytical decisions and model specifications.



Yihan Wang, PhD · honoluluhan717.github.io/yihanwang-site · LinkedIn
